title: What workplace violence prevention training does California require?
description: California Labor Code 6401.9 (SB 553): initial and annual workplace violence training, records, and the pending Cal/OSHA standard, as at November 2026.
shortAnswer: California Labor Code section 6401.9, created by Senate Bill 553 and enforceable since July 1, 2024, requires most California employers to maintain a written Workplace Violence Prevention Plan and to train employees when the plan is first established and annually after that. Training must cover the plan, how to report incidents without retaliation, job-specific hazards and the violent incident log, and must allow interactive questions. Training records must be kept for at least one year.
keyTakeaways: Labor Code 6401.9 applies to most California employers, employees, places of employment and employer-provided housing, except those listed in its subdivision (b).
Employees need initial training and annual refresher training, plus additional training when a new or previously unrecognized hazard is found or the plan changes.
Training must be appropriate to employees' education, literacy and language, and include an opportunity for interactive discussion with someone knowledgeable about the plan.
Training records must be kept for at least one year; hazard records, violent incident logs and incident investigation records for at least five years.
As at November 2026, the Cal/OSHA general industry standard (proposed title 8 section 3343) is still at the advisory committee stage and has not been adopted. The statute applies in the meantime.
regulator: California Division of Occupational Safety and Health (Cal/OSHA), Department of Industrial Relations; Occupational Safety and Health Standards Board (OSHSB)
appliesTo: California employers, employees, places of employment and employer-provided housing, except those listed in Labor Code 6401.9(b)
All employees, including supervisors and managers, covered by the employer's Workplace Violence Prevention Plan
Health care settings are addressed separately by California Code of Regulations, title 8, section 3342 (Violence Prevention in Health Care)

sections.heading: What did SB 553 change for California employers?

blocks.text: SB 553 made a written Workplace Violence Prevention Plan, with training, a legal requirement for most California employers from July 1, 2024. According to Cal/OSHA's [general industry guidance](https://www.dir.ca.gov/dosh/Workplace-Violence/General-Industry.html), Senate Bill 553 (Cortese) was signed into law on September 30, 2023, and Labor Code section 6401.9 became "in effect and enforceable on July 1, 2024."

Cal/OSHA's [employer fact sheet](https://www.dir.ca.gov/dosh/dosh_publications/WPV-General-Industry-for-employers-fs.pdf) explains that SB 553 amended Labor Code section 6401.7 to require employers to develop and implement a plan under the newly codified section 6401.9. The plan may be a stand-alone section of the employer's Injury and Illness Prevention Program under title 8, section 3203, or a separate document. It must be in effect at all times and in all work areas, and be specific to the hazards and corrective measures for each work area and operation.

The statute defines workplace violence as any act of violence or threat of violence that occurs in a place of employment, and sets out four types: Type 1 (by a person with no legitimate business at the worksite), Type 2 (by customers, clients, patients, students, inmates or visitors), Type 3 (by a present or former employee, supervisor or manager), and Type 4 (by a person who has or had a personal relationship with an employee). This page states the position as at November 2026.

sections.heading: What training does Labor Code 6401.9 require?

blocks.text: Employers must provide initial training and annual training after that, with extra training when hazards or the plan change. The Cal/OSHA fact sheet states that "Employers must provide employees with an initial training and annually thereafter" and that training materials must be "easy to understand and match the workers' education, reading skills, and language."

blocks.caption: Required training content under Labor Code 6401.9, as summarized by Cal/OSHA
head: Content area
What employees must learn
rows: The plan
The employer's plan, how to obtain a copy, and how to participate in developing and implementing it.
The law
The definitions and requirements of Labor Code section 6401.9.
Reporting
How to report workplace violence incidents or concerns without fear of retaliation.
Job-specific hazards
Workplace violence hazards specific to their jobs and the corrective and preventive measures in place.
Records
The purpose of the violent incident log and how to obtain copies of related records.
Interaction
An opportunity for interactive questions and answers with a person knowledgeable about the employer's plan.

blocks.text: Additional training is required "when new or previously unidentified workplace violence hazards are discovered, or changes are made to the plan," and it may focus on the specific hazard or plan change. The cycle therefore has three triggers: plan establishment, the annual refresher, and change events. See [how to set mandatory training refresh cycles](/guides/how-to-set-mandatory-training-refresh-cycles).

sections.heading: What must the written plan contain?

blocks.text: The written plan must name who is responsible for it and set procedures covering involvement, reporting, communication, training, hazards, emergencies, investigation and review. Cal/OSHA lists the required elements as:

items: Names or job titles of the persons responsible for implementing the plan.
Procedures for the active involvement of employees and their authorized representatives.
Methods to coordinate implementation with other employers, where applicable.
Procedures to ensure that supervisory and nonsupervisory employees comply with the plan.
Procedures to communicate with and train employees on workplace violence.
Procedures to identify, evaluate and correct workplace violence hazards, including inspections when the plan is first established, periodically, after incidents, and when a new hazard becomes known.
Procedures to respond to actual or potential workplace violence, to accept and respond to reports, and to prohibit retaliation.
Procedures for post-incident response and investigation, and for reviewing the plan annually, when a deficiency becomes apparent, and after an incident.

blocks.text: Because the training must cover the plan itself, plan quality and training quality are linked. Cal/OSHA publishes a [model written plan for general industry](https://www.dir.ca.gov/dosh/dosh_publications/Model-WPV-Plan-General-Industry.docx) that employers can adapt. For turning a written plan into training, see [how to convert policies into training](/guides/how-to-convert-policies-into-training).

sections.heading: What training records must employers keep?

blocks.text: Training records must be created and kept for at least one year, which is shorter than the five-year retention for the other workplace violence records. Cal/OSHA's guidance sets these minimums:

blocks.caption: Minimum record retention under Labor Code 6401.9, as stated by Cal/OSHA
head: Record
Minimum retention
rows: Workplace violence prevention plan training records
1 year
Hazard identification, evaluation and correction records
5 years
Violent incident logs
5 years
Workplace violence incident investigation records
5 years

blocks.text: Cal/OSHA's model plan says training records should include training dates, contents or a summary of the sessions, names and qualifications of the persons conducting the training, and names and job titles of all attendees. Records, including training records and violent incident logs, must be made available to employees and their authorized representatives on request, without cost, for examination and copying within 15 calendar days. Keeping training records for longer than the one-year minimum makes it easier to show an unbroken annual history. See [how to prepare training records for an audit](/guides/how-to-prepare-training-records-for-an-audit).

sections.heading: Has Cal/OSHA adopted a workplace violence standard for general industry?

blocks.text: Not as at November 2026. Cal/OSHA's general industry page states that the Division would submit a standard to the Occupational Safety and Health Standards Board no later than December 31, 2025, and that the Board "is required to adopt the standard no later than December 31, 2026." That page was last updated on March 19, 2024.

blocks.title: Status as at November 2026: standard still in development
blocks.text: Cal/OSHA's [advisory committee page](https://www.dir.ca.gov/dosh/doshreg/Workplace-Violence-in-General-Industry/) for proposed title 8 section 3343, Workplace Violence Prevention in General Industry, shows revised discussion drafts in April and July 2026, a September 2026 discussion draft, and an in-person advisory meeting on October 27, 2026. The Standards Board's [proposed regulations list](https://www.dir.ca.gov/oshsb/proposedregulations.html), updated October 2026, does not include a workplace violence rulemaking notice. Employers should comply with Labor Code 6401.9 now and watch for a formal rulemaking notice, which the Standards Board follows with a public hearing before it votes on adoption.

When a standard is adopted, its training provisions may add detail beyond the statute. Employers that build their training around a clear mapping of requirements to content will find it easier to update when the final text is published. See [how to update training when regulations change](/guides/how-to-update-training-when-regulations-change).

sections.heading: How can employers map the requirements to outcomes and evidence?

blocks.text: Map each required content area to an outcome and to evidence that would satisfy a Cal/OSHA inspector or an employee records request. The mapping below is illustrative.

blocks.caption: Illustrative mapping: Labor Code 6401.9 training to learning outcome to evidence
head: Requirement
Example learning outcome
Evidence to retain
rows: Plan familiarity
Locates the plan and explains how to take part in reviewing it.
Attendance record with plan version and date.
Reporting without retaliation
Reports a threat through the designated channel and knows retaliation is prohibited.
Scenario check results and the reporting procedure version taught.
Job-specific hazards
Identifies the main violence risks in their role, such as cash handling or working alone, and the controls in place.
Role-specific module completion linked to the hazard assessment.
Interactive Q&A
Raises questions and receives answers from a person knowledgeable about the plan.
Session notes or logged questions with responses and trainer name and qualifications.
Change-triggered training
Applies a new control introduced after an incident.
Incident or hazard record linked to the additional training delivered.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry links each training element to the plan version, the hazard assessment items for each role, and the assessment points that evidence understanding. When the plan changes or a new hazard is recorded, the roles needing additional training can be identified from those links. See [operational procedures programs](/programs/operational-procedures) for how this is applied.

faqs.q: Does SB 553 apply to remote workers?
faqs.a: Labor Code 6401.9 applies to employers, employees and places of employment except those listed in subdivision (b), which contains specific exclusions. Employers with remote staff should read subdivision (b) in the statute itself to confirm whether particular employees or locations are excluded, rather than assuming that all remote work is in or out of scope.

faqs.q: Can workplace violence training be delivered online?
faqs.a: The statute summary from Cal/OSHA requires an opportunity for interactive questions and answers with a person knowledgeable about the employer's plan. An online course alone, with no way to ask questions and receive answers, would not meet that element. Online modules combined with a live or responsive question channel can address this.

faqs.q: How often must workplace violence training be repeated?
faqs.a: Annually. Employers must provide initial training when the plan is first established and annual training after that. Additional training is also required when new or previously unrecognized hazards are found or the plan changes, and it may be limited to the new hazard or the change.

faqs.q: Do health care employers follow Labor Code 6401.9?
faqs.a: Health care settings have their own Cal/OSHA standard, title 8 section 3342 (Violence Prevention in Health Care), which Cal/OSHA lists separately from the general industry requirements. Health care employers should confirm which requirements apply to each of their locations, especially for non-clinical sites such as administrative offices.
